title: Costume Contest

jokes.text: Someone is wearing/using something that isn't theirs — 'That's not yours.'
jokes.setup: A character is enthusiastically showing off something ('It's kind of badass, right?') with confidence.
jokes.punchline: A flat, matter-of-fact correction: 'That's not yours.' Deflating the bravado instantly.
jokes.explanation: A clean economy-of-words deflation joke. The confidence of the setup makes the flat correction land, but without character attribution it's generic.

jokes.text: Someone drank something that wasn't their hot coffee and didn't realize it — 'Is there no limit to what he won't notice?'
jokes.setup: A character apparently drank the wrong drink and didn't register it.
jokes.punchline: The rhetorical question: 'Is there no limit to what he won't notice?' — framing obliviousness as an almost impressive trait.
jokes.explanation: Works as a talking-head observation about an oblivious coworker. The double negative construction ('no limit to what he won't notice') is a slight grammatical twist that adds dry wit, but the setup is incomplete in transcript form.

jokes.text: Crossword puzzle answer: 'Handbag' — 'What's a seven-letter word for [blank]? No, starts with an H.' / 'Handbag.'
jokes.setup: Someone is stuck on a crossword clue, asking for a seven-letter word, specifying it starts with H.
jokes.punchline: Another character immediately supplies 'Handbag' as if it's obvious — the joke being the mundanity or the confidence of the answer.
jokes.explanation: A mild bit of workplace texture humor. The transcript is incomplete so the full comedic value is unclear, but the beat feels like Stanley doing a crossword puzzle while tuning out an office meeting — a recurring character gag. Functional but not strong.

jokes.text: Michael announces 'our branch on the planet Jupiter is up 8,000% in sales.'
jokes.setup: Michael calls a meeting, asking everyone to take a seat, implying serious business news.
jokes.punchline: He announces their 'branch on planet Jupiter' is up 8,000% in sales — complete nonsense delivered with managerial authority.
jokes.explanation: Pure Michael Scott — he creates gravitas around a meeting only to say something completely unhinged with total sincerity. The specificity of '8,000%' and 'planet Jupiter' elevates it from generic absurdism to character-specific comedy. Only Michael would announce this deadpan.

jokes.text: Stanley checks the clock mid-meeting: 'Hold up. That clock is slow. It is 5:00. I will see you all tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Michael is mid-sentence delivering meeting content. Stanley checks the clock.
jokes.punchline: Stanley announces with complete authority that it's 5:00 and walks out, mid-meeting, without hesitation.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Stanley joke. His utter disregard for Michael's authority and his laser focus on clocking out exactly at 5:00 is one of the show's most reliable character-comedy engines. 'I will see you all tomorrow' — delivered with the gravity of a CEO departing — is excellent economy. High character integration: no other character on the show could deliver this with the same weight.

jokes.text: Kevin says his costume makes him look like Michael Moore.
jokes.setup: Oscar asks Kevin what statement he's making with his costume.
jokes.punchline: Kevin reveals, with sincerity, that he thinks he kind of looks like Michael Moore — implying his 'costume' is just being himself.
jokes.explanation: Classic Kevin self-own. He genuinely believes he looks like Michael Moore, which is both a self-deprecating joke and a window into his sincere, unironic nature. The implicit joke — his 'costume' requires no effort — is well-integrated into his character.

jokes.text: Erin answers the phone: 'Dunder-Mifflin, this is Erin. Happy Halloween. How can I haunt you today?'
jokes.setup: Standard receptionist phone greeting.
jokes.punchline: Erin substitutes 'help' with 'haunt' — 'How can I haunt you today?' — delivered with sincere cheerfulness.
jokes.explanation: Simple wordplay executed with perfect Erin energy — she's genuinely delighted by it. The character integration is strong because Erin would be the only Dunder Mifflin receptionist who would do this so earnestly. The pun itself is mild but the delivery sells it.

jokes.text: MacGruber SNL countdown interrupts Erin's talking head — 'Six seconds, MacGruber! / Two seconds, MacGruber! / Oh, boom! Ohh, explosion! MacGruber!'
jokes.setup: Erin is giving a straightforward talking-head about Halloween activities.
jokes.punchline: A MacGruber countdown randomly erupts and explodes, interrupting her monologue multiple times — Erin seems unbothered.
jokes.explanation: A slightly chaotic bit — the MacGruber interruptions are absurdist and suggest someone off-screen is doing an impression, but the transcript makes it murky. Works as background office chaos on Halloween but doesn't build to much.

jokes.text: The 2011 Scranton/Wilkes-Barre coupon book is revealed as the costume contest prize, 'worth over $15,000 in savings.'
jokes.setup: Erin builds up the prize dramatically: 'Might have something to do with the prize. Maybe you've heard of it.'
jokes.punchline: The prize is a coupon book — treated with the reverence of a luxury vacation.
jokes.explanation: The setup is nicely structured — Erin builds anticipation for the prize reveal the same way a game show host would, which makes the mundane punchline funnier. Sets up the running gag about Oscar's rational consumer analysis later.

jokes.text: Dwight in a Scranton Strangler costume: 'If I was the real Scranton Strangler, you'd be so strangled by now.' Then: 'And if you're out there, strangler, you will get caught. By me.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is dressed as (or referencing) the Scranton Strangler, a local serial killer, as a Halloween costume.
jokes.punchline: He simultaneously threatens someone in character AND breaks character to address the real strangler directly with vigilante bravado.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight joke. The pivot from threatening someone as the Strangler to suddenly addressing the real Strangler directly is a perfect double-character beat — it shows his costume choice, his self-seriousness, and his Schrute-ian sense of justice all at once. Only Dwight would dress as a serial killer AND use the moment to issue a warning to said serial killer. The 'By me' tag is perfectly economical. Near-exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Someone's talking head: 'Sounds like someone's really trying to convince us that he's not the Scranton Strangler.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just vowed to catch the Scranton Strangler.
jokes.punchline: A talking-head observation that Dwight's intensity suggests he might actually BE the Strangler.
jokes.explanation: A sharp observational callback. The talking-head structure makes it land as deadpan commentary. The implication — Dwight doth protest too much — is both funny and plays into the show's running Scranton Strangler subplot.

jokes.text: Creed's talking head: 'To my chickens, I'm the Scranton Strangler.'
jokes.setup: The Scranton Strangler is being discussed as a local threat.
jokes.punchline: Creed casually reveals he strangles his chickens, equating himself with a serial killer with complete nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. In eight words, it perfectly encapsulates Creed Bratton as a character — the cheerful admission of something deeply unsettling, delivered as if it's a reasonable point of comparison. The escalation from 'Dwight might be the Strangler' to 'Creed admits to being a domestic strangler' is beautifully structured. Maximum economy. Quintessential Creed — this joke could not be said by any other character on television. Strong contender for the episode's top joke.

jokes.text: Dwight mistakes Pam's Olive Oyl costume for Dwight Schrute's mom: 'Looks like someone decided to dress up as ol' Dwight Schrute's mom.'
jokes.setup: Pam is dressed as Olive Oyl (from Popeye), waiting for Jim to wear his Popeye costume.
jokes.punchline: Dwight confidently identifies her as his own mother — 'You're only 1/3 as beautiful and about half her height.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight bit. The insult — 'You're only 1/3 as beautiful and about half her height' — is precisely calibrated Dwight-style criticism, simultaneously insulting Pam AND inexplicably reverent toward his own mother. The specific fractions are very Dwight. The misdirection (we expect him to identify the actual costume) leads to an absurd alternative that reveals character.

jokes.text: Dwight tells Pam she looks like 'ol' Dwight Schrute's mom' — 'You're only 1/3 as beautiful and about half her height.'
jokes.setup: Pam is dressed as Olive Oyl; Dwight insults her costume
jokes.punchline: The insult backhands itself — Dwight is defending his mother's honor by saying Pam is a poor substitute, which also means Dwight thinks his mom is beautiful
jokes.explanation: Dwight insulting someone while inadvertently complimenting his own mother is a subtle character touch — his loyalty to the Schrute family bleeds into every interaction. '1/3 as beautiful' is an amusingly precise metric.

jokes.text: Pam explains that Jim refuses to wear his Popeye costume. Jim in talking head: 'I've never really been a costume guy. Even when I was a kid, it just felt like something I was too old for.'
jokes.setup: Pam explains her Olive Oyl costume only makes sense next to Popeye, but Jim won't wear his costume.
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking head rationalizes it as a lifelong maturity stance — 'it just felt like something I was too old for' — which is clearly him being a wet blanket on Halloween.
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke — Jim's self-flattering explanation for being a Halloween killjoy is very 'Jim,' but it's also slightly a character regression from prior seasons where he was enthusiastic about pranks. Works as a comedic setup for Pam forcing him into costume later.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head poker face reaction to Pam handing him the Popeye costume: 'In case you can't read my poker face...' — cut before he finishes.
jokes.setup: Jim has been explaining he's 'not a costume guy.' Pam hands him his costume.
jokes.punchline: He starts referencing his own poker face — implying his disgust is visible — and the cut implies the audience can read it perfectly well.
jokes.explanation: A good Jim talking-head moment. The partial sentence cut is a mockumentary editing joke — the show implies Jim's expression finishes the sentence. Works best with the visual.

jokes.text: Someone doing a MacGruber impression during what appears to be Gabe's policy presentation: 'I have ten seconds to explain them or this whole place blows up. MacGruber! Lame.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is making a dry presentation about sales policies.
jokes.punchline: Someone undercuts the presentation with MacGruber urgency, and the response is simply: 'Lame.'
jokes.explanation: The MacGruber gag is wearing thin by its third iteration. 'Lame' as the response is meta-commentary on the joke itself, which is a bit too self-aware to be effective. Running gag without escalation.

jokes.text: Creed's witch joke: 'Why don't witches wear panties? Because they need to grip the broom.'
jokes.setup: A costume party atmosphere. Creed delivers a classic dirty joke.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is an old-fashioned vulgar joke about witches and broomsticks.
jokes.explanation: An old joke, but appropriate for Creed as a character — he would tell old, off-color jokes. The prefacing 'Oh, here we go' from a coworker suggests this is familiar Creed territory. Low originality but high character fit. Functional.

jokes.text: The Dracula water-ski joke mangled in real time: 'Oh! Who likes to water-ski on Lake Erie? No, what... Where does Dracula like to water ski? Lake Erie.'
jokes.setup: Someone attempts a Halloween-themed joke about Dracula.
jokes.punchline: They stumble over the setup, lose the structure, then deliver the punchline anyway — 'Lake Erie' — as if the botched delivery didn't happen. The joke itself is also weak (Erie/eerie).
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is the botched delivery rather than the pun itself. 'Lake Erie/eerie' is a mild pun, but watching someone fumble the setup before soldiering through to the punchline is cringe-comedy gold in a low-key way. Works better on screen than in transcript.

jokes.text: Andy calls Gabe 'Gabe-wad' to his face.
jokes.setup: Gabe is presenting corporate policy changes with straight-laced authority.
jokes.punchline: Andy asks 'Has anyone started calling you Gabe-wad yet?' — directly to Gabe, who says 'Not here, no.' Andy then just says 'Gabe-wad.'
jokes.explanation: A very Andy move — socially unaware enough to call his boss a name to his face, then double down when corrected. The structure (question → denial → just saying it anyway) is tight. Gabe's flat 'Not here, no' is the perfect straight-man response. The repetition of 'Gabe-wad' as the final beat is economical and funny.

jokes.text: Jim recognizes Darryl's idea: 'That's like exactly sort of the idea that you had.' Darryl: 'Yes, I do remember saying something like that to you.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has just 'casually' shared that corporate is implementing a delivery-sales plan.
jokes.punchline: Jim gently points out it was Darryl's idea. Darryl's faux-casual 'Yes, I do remember saying something like that' is a masterclass in understated acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: Darryl's deadpan understatement — 'I do remember saying something like that' — is a good line. His performative casualness while clearly plotting is strong character work.

jokes.text: Jim apologizes to Darryl. Darryl: 'I'm just glad we're gonna try it out.' Jim: 'Really? We're good? We're cool.' Darryl: 'Okay.' Then Darryl notices: 'What's that in your shirt?' Jim: 'Oh, that's a ream of paper. Thought you might hit me.'
jokes.setup: Jim is apologizing to Darryl for blocking his idea. The conversation seems to be resolving warmly.
jokes.punchline: Jim has stuffed a ream of paper in his shirt as padding in case Darryl punched him — the most over-engineered conflict-avoidance strategy imaginable.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent physical comedy reveal. Jim wearing a ream of paper as body armor is perfectly absurd and perfectly Jim — self-aware enough to know he might deserve to be hit, neurotic enough to prepare for it. The escalation from warm reconciliation to 'Thought you might hit me' is perfectly timed. High character integration (this is very Jim Halpert behavior) and excellent structure.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head about Darryl: 'Darryl Philbin is the greatest guy in the world. And you know what I'd like? I would like to have all the racists brought together and take Darryl Philbin out to lunch. Just to see what they're missing.'
jokes.setup: Michael is expressing his admiration for Darryl.
jokes.punchline: His expression of fondness involves gathering 'all the racists' for a lunch outing — a completely unhinged plan delivered with total sincerity and warmth.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. Michael Scott at his most Michael Scott — he genuinely loves Darryl and wants to share that love with 'all the racists' as a corrective educational lunch. The logic is both offensive and oddly sweet, which is the narrow lane Michael Scott inhabits best. Only Steve Carell/Michael Scott can make this land as endearing rather than simply awful. The construction is tight and the escalation within the sentence is superb. Comparable to the anchor examples for character specificity and originality.

jokes.text: Oscar debunks the coupon book prize: 'Everyone realizes this coupon book is not actually worth $15,000, right? You'd have to spend $200,000 on crap you don't even need to get $15,000 worth of benefits.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is excited about the coupon book worth '$15,000 in savings.'
jokes.punchline: Oscar does rapid math and exposes the coupon book as requiring $200,000 in spending to yield $15,000 back — not a prize worth fighting over.
jokes.explanation: A very Oscar moment — his rational-consumer analysis is perfectly in character. The specificity of the math ($200,000 spend for $15,000 benefit) elevates this from mere skepticism to something genuinely clever. Sets up Oscar's 'rational consumer' costume gag later. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: When colleagues agree with Oscar that the coupon book is a bad deal, Kelly shuts it down: 'Yeah, shut it, Oscar. Pam. This is an amazing prize.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just logically demolished the value of the coupon book prize.
jokes.punchline: Kelly dismisses his entirely correct analysis with 'Yeah, shut it, Oscar' and doubles down on her desire for the coupon book.
jokes.explanation: Kelly's blind enthusiasm vs. Oscar's pragmatism is a reliable comedy engine. 'Shut it, Oscar' is a great line in its bluntness — she doesn't refute his math, she just refuses to engage with it. Very true to Kelly's character.

jokes.text: Kevin is whispering with Gabe — Michael panics. Dwight: 'Probably about the extremes of the human physique.'
jokes.setup: Michael is paranoid that Kevin is going 'over his head' to Gabe. Kevin and Gabe are whispering.
jokes.punchline: Dwight offers his assessment — they're probably discussing 'the extremes of the human physique,' a reference to Kevin and Gabe's very different body types — with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: One of Dwight's best lines in the episode. 'Extremes of the human physique' is a brilliant Dwight-ism — technically neutral language used to comment on Kevin's weight and Gabe's skinniness without being a crude fat joke. The clinical phrasing is very Dwight. High economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Michael confronts Kevin for going over his head — it turns out Kevin was just showing Gabe a Lady Gaga robot dance move.
jokes.setup: Michael has worked himself into a fury about Kevin bypassing the chain of command.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's 'transgression' was telling Gabe about a Lady Gaga dance move where she 'powers down like a robot' for the costume contest catwalk.
jokes.explanation: Classic Office misdirection — an entire subplot of managerial anxiety deflates when the 'corporate conspiracy' turns out to be Kevin sharing a dance move. The reveal is well-structured. Michael's overreaction compared to the innocuous reality is the core comedy engine here, very characteristic of the show at its best.

jokes.text: Jim continues: 'We were basically Romeo and Juliet. Except where Juliet doesn't have that great a time, and Romeo doesn't call back after two dates.'
jokes.setup: Jim sets up the Romeo and Juliet comparison to seem grandiose
jokes.punchline: He immediately dismantles it with the specific, mundane reality — 'Juliet doesn't have that great a time, and Romeo doesn't call back after two dates'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is clean: 'Romeo and Juliet' sets an expectation, and the punchline replaces the tragedy with two extremely mundane disappointments. 'Doesn't have that great a time' is the understated version of the entire Romeo/Juliet tragedy applied to a mediocre date. 'Doesn't call back after two dates' is the modern-day equivalent of death. Structure is near-perfect: setup, elevation, precise subversion. Quotable and highly specific.

jokes.text: Gossip about Jim and Pam's reaction to Danny's party: 'Jim and Pam basically begged us not to go.' / 'Or you're dead.'
jokes.setup: Ryan and Kelly tell Danny that Jim and Pam 'begged' them not to attend his party, and add 'don't tell them we said anything. Or you're dead.'
jokes.punchline: The transparent manipulation ('don't tell them or you're dead') makes it clear they're manufacturing drama, not conveying a sincere message.
jokes.explanation: Ryan and Kelly stirring drama is on-brand, though the 'or you're dead' tag is the most memorable part. Functional workplace-politics comedy.

jokes.text: Michael says he'll never forget what Danny did to Pam: 'I forget nothing. I'm like an elephant in that way.' Then immediately fumbles an elephant metaphor.
jokes.setup: Michael is expressing loyalty to Jim regarding Danny's history with Pam.
jokes.punchline: He compares himself to an elephant for his memory, then immediately starts to unpack the metaphor ('You know what eleph... buh... this...') and it collapses.
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-undermining rhetoric is a reliable comedic mechanism. He makes a strong declarative statement and then immediately botches the metaphor he was using to support it. The trailing 'buh... this... this sucks for Jim, right?' pivot is very authentic Michael. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Ryan and Kelly discuss not getting invited to parties: 'This sucks for Jim, right? But it also sucks for us, because we don't get invited to a ton of Halloween parties.'
jokes.setup: They're supposedly expressing sympathy for Jim's awkward situation with Danny.
jokes.punchline: The real concern quickly emerges: they themselves don't get invited to many Halloween parties, so missing Danny's is a genuine loss for them.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'this sucks for Jim' to 'but also sucks for us' is a nice self-interested character beat. Ryan and Kelly's social anxiety about not being popular is character-consistent.

jokes.text: Party guest list: 'Stanley, Phyllis, Angela, Darryl, Creed's a maybe.' / 'Creed's going?'
jokes.setup: Ryan and Kelly are listing who will be at Danny's party.
jokes.punchline: 'Creed's a maybe' is treated as weighty information — the reaction 'Creed's going?' suggests Creed's presence at a social event is surprising and notable.
jokes.explanation: A small Creed joke — the implication is that Creed attending a normal social event is an alarming prospect. Works as quick background character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael has Erin put Darryl on speakerphone — Darryl says 'I'm good' instead of coming out to the office.
jokes.setup: Michael dramatically summons Darryl to the main office to celebrate his idea.
jokes.punchline: Darryl, still on the phone, simply says 'I'm good' — declining the honor of being publicly celebrated.
jokes.explanation: Darryl's flat refusal — 'I'm good' — when Michael is trying to build a ceremonial moment is a perfect Darryl response. The two-word dismissal of Michael's grandiosity is very economical.

jokes.text: Michael to Darryl: 'You need to stop being so shy. Come out here and embrace who you really are, Superstar.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has said 'I'm good' and declined to come out.
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets Darryl's reluctance as shyness and encourages him to 'embrace who he really is.' Darryl: 'This is embarrassing, Michael.' Michael: 'Yeah, I bet it is.'
jokes.explanation: Michael's response — 'Yeah, I bet it is' — is inadvertently correct but for the wrong reasons. Michael thinks Darryl is embarrassed by his own modesty; Darryl is embarrassed by Michael's spectacle. The miscommunication is very Office. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael can't figure out how to use the speakerphone: 'Um, hit the speakerphone button. The speakerphone button? Same button as you hit before. Or sit on it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to make a dramatic speakerphone moment happen.
jokes.punchline: He can't figure out which button to press, and someone unhelpfully suggests he 'sit on it' — the moment deflates into tech confusion.
jokes.explanation: Mild tech-incompetence humor. Works as character texture for Michael but isn't a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: Michael's big speech about screwing corporate — then Darryl cuts him off: 'Corporate stole nothing. Okay? Darryl brought this idea to me, and then I told them, giving Darryl full credit. So no need to screw corporate.'
jokes.setup: Michael has worked up a heroic 'screw corporate!' speech to champion Darryl.
jokes.punchline: Darryl calmly explains that Michael already got credit for the idea properly — completely deflating Michael's martyrdom narrative.
jokes.explanation: The classic Office comedic structure: Michael builds to an emotional climax, only for reality to make it immediately unnecessary. The deflation is well-timed. 'So no need to screw corporate' is the perfect antihero button.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'I'm a little peeved at Darryl right now. He went to Gabe behind your back.' Dwight: 'No, he didn't go behind my back, he went over my head.' Michael: 'He went over your head to go behind your back.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight are discussing Darryl's maneuver using anatomical directional metaphors.
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'He went over your head to go behind your back' — a nonsensical but confident corporate jargon mashup that Dwight immediately validates.
jokes.explanation: A great wordplay moment. Michael's 'over your head to go behind your back' is geometrically absurd corporate-speak, yet delivered with Michael's unshakeable confidence. The construction is tight and quotable. Dwight's earnest engagement with the nonsense elevates it. Strong character integration — this exact brand of jargon-soup is Michael's dialect.

jokes.text: Michael: 'What is taking someone from behind?' — as an innocent follow-up to the corporate metaphors.
jokes.setup: They're discussing 'going behind someone's back' in corporate hierarchy terms.
jokes.punchline: Michael asks 'What is taking someone from behind?' with complete innocence — the double entendre is entirely unintentional on his part.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Michael Scott unintentional double entendre. The fact that he genuinely means it as a corporate question makes it better. Dwight's 'No, shh, Michael, listen' suggests Dwight catches the implication before Michael does, which adds a layer. Very economical — the line is six words and contains multitudes.

jokes.text: Michael: 'We need to strangle Darryl's idea.'
jokes.setup: They're discussing how to shut down Darryl's corporate ambitions.
jokes.punchline: Given that the Scranton Strangler has just been discussed, Michael's choice of the word 'strangle' is grimly funny.
jokes.explanation: Whether intentional or not, using 'strangle' in an episode saturated with Scranton Strangler references is a nice dark touch. Functions as both corporate jargon and a callback to earlier jokes. Short and punchy.

jokes.text: Kelly changes her costume mid-day. Pam: 'Kelly! You cannot change costumes in the middle of the day!' / 'Pam, she's out.' / Kelly: 'Um, if I'm out, I'm gonna sue this entire company for discrimination!'
jokes.setup: The costume contest is in progress. Kelly changes her costume, apparently seeking a competitive advantage.
jokes.punchline: Kelly immediately threatens to sue for discrimination if she's disqualified — a wildly disproportionate legal escalation over a Halloween costume contest.
jokes.explanation: Extremely Kelly. Her instant escalation to litigation over a coupon book costume contest is character-perfect. 'I'm gonna sue this entire company for discrimination' over a Halloween party rule is the kind of disproportionate reaction that defines Kelly Kapoor. The silliness of what she's threatening to sue over makes it very funny.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Guys, you're arguing over a 1 in 16 chance. Over a prize worth... 40 bucks.' / Kelly: 'Um, 15,000 bucks, Oscar.'
jokes.setup: The costume contest has devolved into an argument.
jokes.punchline: Oscar reframes the prize's actual value as ~$40 based on his earlier math. Kelly corrects him with the face-value number, missing the entire point.
jokes.explanation: A great callback payoff. Oscar's analytical approach ('40 bucks') vs. Kelly's face-value thinking ('15,000 bucks, Oscar') captures their character dynamic perfectly. Oscar's sigh of '40 bucks' is excellent deadpan.

jokes.text: Angela explains she's dressed as a nurse because they were sold out of other costumes: 'Look, they were sold out of all the other costumes, okay? Think we all live in the real world here. Let's not pretend to be unaware of what sells in this office.'
jokes.setup: Angela is dressed as a sexy nurse — unexpected for the famously prudish Angela.
jokes.punchline: Her defensive explanation — 'let's not pretend to be unaware of what sells' — reveals she knew exactly what she was doing and is in denial about it.
jokes.explanation: An Angela joke that works on multiple levels: the absurdity of prudish Angela in a sexy nurse costume, and her elaborate rationalization ('sold out of all the other costumes') that's clearly a lie. 'Let's not pretend to be unaware of what sells in this office' is both self-aware and completely delusional. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: Michael dressed as Darryl, confronting Darryl directly at the costume catwalk: 'Do you know who I am? Happy Halloween, jerk!'
jokes.setup: Michael, angry at Darryl for going over his head, has dressed as Darryl as a passive-aggressive Halloween statement.
jokes.punchline: He confronts Darryl in costume with 'Happy Halloween, jerk!' — as if the costume itself is a devastating insult.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott passive-aggression taken to its logical extreme — dressing as your nemesis for Halloween to make a 'statement.' The 'Happy Halloween, jerk!' delivery is perfectly unhinged. The joke is that Michael thinks this is devastating while it's just sad and bizarre.

jokes.text: Michael: 'This whole going-over-my-head-gate is making people act weird. Chain of command is crumbling. Do you know what just happened? I just made Kevin cry. And Gabe looks like Lady Gaga. That's not Halloween.'
jokes.setup: Michael is tallying the day's damage from his chain-of-command crusade
jokes.punchline: 'Gabe looks like Lady Gaga. That's not Halloween.' — Michael's bizarre conclusion that Lady Gaga is somehow not a Halloween-appropriate costume
jokes.explanation: Michael's moral framework — 'Halloween should honor monsters, not make people mad' — is a wonderful distillation of his character. The pivot from 'chain of command is crumbling' to 'Gabe looks like Lady Gaga, that's not Halloween' is perfect Michael logic: the real tragedy is the aesthetic mismatch, not the workplace drama. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'I guess you could say I'm still in costume. I'm a rational consumer.' / 'Yeah, I heard you say it to Phyllis.' / 'That's a good line.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is apparently trying out his 'rational consumer' costume concept on multiple people before the catwalk.
jokes.punchline: Someone has already heard him say it to Phyllis — Oscar's self-satisfied repetition of the same line undercuts the bit.
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke about Oscar being caught recycling his own punchline is a nice layer. 'That's a good line' delivered to yourself is a very Oscar moment of self-congratulation. Works well as a building block to the catwalk payoff.

jokes.text: Michael continues in his Darryl costume at the catwalk: 'Still don't know who I am? I'll give you a hint. I go over other people's heads.'
jokes.setup: Michael is dressed as Darryl and parading around.
jokes.punchline: His 'hint' — 'I go over other people's heads' — reveals that this entire costume choice is about punishing Darryl publicly.
jokes.explanation: Callback to the 'over my head' corporate language. Michael weaponizing costume-guessing to air workplace grievances is deeply Michael.

jokes.text: Gabe does the Lady Gaga robot power-down move on the costume catwalk.
jokes.setup: Kevin taught Gabe a Lady Gaga dance move for the catwalk — the earlier 'Kevin going over Michael's head' subplot.
jokes.punchline: The payoff is Gabe actually executing the robot power-down on the catwalk, in full costume.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Lady Gaga subplot — Gabe actually doing the move is the structural completion of a joke that's been building. Works as both a visual gag and callback. Gabe is an inherently funny physical presence for this type of moment.

jokes.text: Oscar walks the catwalk with a sign: 'The Rational Consumer' — and is presented by Pam: 'I present to you the Rational Consumer. As it were.'
jokes.setup: Oscar debunked the coupon book prize earlier. Now the costume contest catwalk is happening.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's costume is 'The Rational Consumer' — meta-commentary on his own behavior earlier in the episode.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully self-aware joke. Oscar's costume is the punchline to his own character arc in the episode. 'I'm a rational consumer' as a Halloween costume is absurdist but also deeply Oscar-correct. The payoff of Pam saying 'As it were' captures the mild awkwardness of it. This is smart structural comedy — Oscar's costume IS the episode's coupon book gag tied up in a bow.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I know how to sit on a fence. Hell, I can even sleep on a fence. The trick is to do it face down with the post in your mouth.'
jokes.setup: Darryl accuses Dwight of not taking sides in the Michael/Darryl dispute.
jokes.punchline: Dwight responds with a detailed explanation of his literal fence-sitting capability, including the technique of sleeping on a fence 'face down with the post in your mouth.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Dwight's literal interpretation of 'sitting on the fence' — and his expertise at it — is perfectly absurd and perfectly Dwight. The technique detail ('face down with the post in your mouth') is wonderfully specific and unexpected. This is textbook Dwight: taking a figurative expression at face value and then demonstrating genuine competence at the literal version. High originality, high character integration, highly quotable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor example for the combination of unexpectedness and economy.

jokes.text: Ouija board spells out 'A-S-S': Michael's question to the spirit world was whether Darryl is a bad friend, and the Ouija board begins spelling out a word. Michael reads: 'A... S... S...' then deflects: 'H... E... T. An asset. Aah!'
jokes.setup: Michael asks the Ouija board if Darryl is a bad friend. The board begins spelling out a word starting with A-S-S.
jokes.punchline: Michael quickly redirects the spelling to 'asset' — clearly changing course when he realizes where it's going. The scream after confirms he knows.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed bit. The setup has genuine comedic tension as the Ouija board slowly spells out A-S-S, and Michael's pivot to 'asset' is a great character save — he wants to believe in the supernatural but also controls the narrative. The shriek is the perfect button. Strong structure with genuine payoff.

jokes.text: Ouija board spells out 'A-S-S...' and the group debates whether it's going to spell 'asshat' — it spells 'asset.'
jokes.setup: The Ouija board begins spelling out a response to the question about Darryl; it appears to be spelling a vulgar word
jokes.punchline: It spells 'asset' — the misdirect is the expectation of an insult, resolved by a genuinely positive word
jokes.explanation: A clean misdirection. The letters A-S-S lead the audience and characters toward a profane conclusion; 'asset' is the subversion that works both as a punchline and as a character beat (Darryl moved the planchette, vindicating himself). The 'Aah! Aah!' panic reaction before the reveal adds physical comedy.

jokes.text: Jim asks Danny why he never called Pam back. Danny claims 'her fours looked like eights.' Jim: 'But you also called her the second time, so you had the number right.'
jokes.setup: Danny says he lost Pam's number because her handwriting made fours look like eights.
jokes.punchline: Jim points out that Danny called a second time — meaning he had the number right — calmly dismantling the excuse.
jokes.explanation: A great Jim moment. He dismantles Danny's excuse with gentle, Sherlock-esque logic ('you called a second time, so you had the number right') without raising his voice. The measured way Jim exposes the lie while clearly deeply caring about the outcome is very authentic Jim Halpert. Tight structure, high character integration.

jokes.text: Danny: 'Halpert, you looking for someone to bang your wife?' Jim: 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Jim is pressing Danny about why he didn't call Pam back — it's coming across as protective/jealous.
jokes.punchline: Danny cuts through it: 'You looking for someone to bang your wife?' Jim's flat 'Nope' refuses to engage with the provocation.
jokes.explanation: The bluntness of Danny's question and Jim's monosyllabic 'Nope' is very funny. The question cuts through four scenes of elaborate social maneuvering with crude directness, and Jim's calm denial is the best possible response. Economy is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Danny reveals he didn't call Pam back because 'she spent the whole date talking about you [Jim]. She was obviously in love with you.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been demanding to know the real reason Danny didn't call Pam back
jokes.punchline: The reason is that Pam was already in love with Jim during their date — Jim's pursuit of this answer comes full circle to incriminate him as the reason Pam wasn't available
jokes.explanation: A strong narrative and comedic payoff. The revelation that Jim is the reason Pam wasn't available — making Jim both the cause and beneficiary of the ghosting — is satisfying both dramatically and comedically. The irony that Jim's interrogation uncovers his own role is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Danny reveals why he didn't call Pam back: 'I didn't call her back because she spent the whole date talking about you. She was obviously in love with you.'
jokes.setup: Jim has been pursuing the reason Danny didn't call Pam back, clearly expecting something unflattering about Pam.
jokes.punchline: The reason was that Pam was so obviously in love with Jim that Danny saw no point in calling — a genuinely sweet revelation dressed as a comedic payoff.
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent misdirection — we expect something bad about Pam, we get something that validates Jim and Pam's entire relationship. Lands as both funny and emotionally resonant, which is The Office at its best. The subversion is unexpected and earned.

jokes.text: Erin is bobbing for apples during the party scene — turns out she ate two whole apples: '57, 58. Wait, she hasn't moved in a while. Erin. Er... Two. I got two. I ate two whole apples.'
jokes.setup: Erin is bobbing for apples. Someone is counting seconds.
jokes.punchline: After nearly a minute submerged, Erin surfaces having eaten two entire apples while underwater — presented with complete pride.
jokes.explanation: Delightfully absurd Erin moment. The escalating concern ('she hasn't moved in a while') followed by Erin surfacing triumphant having consumed two whole apples is perfectly Erin — sincere, physically committed, missing the social point entirely. High character integration; this is exactly how Erin would approach bobbing for apples.

jokes.text: Danny's real reason for not calling Pam back: 'I didn't call you back 'cause I thought you seemed a little... dorky.'
jokes.setup: Pam insists she'd remember talking about Jim on the date, pushing Danny for the real reason. The expectation is something serious.
jokes.punchline: A long pause, then: 'Dorky.' Simple, honest, deflating.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. The entire subplot has built toward this answer, which is simultaneously deflating, funny, and a little painful. The pause before 'dorky' is crucial — all that buildup for the most mundane, honest answer possible. Pam's 'Thank you. I got it. Now I know.' makes it even better — she's not devastated, just finally at peace. The economy is exceptional: one word delivers the entire punchline. Strong structure — the setup has been running for eight minutes.

jokes.text: Danny tells Pam the real reason he didn't call back: '...Dorky.' Beat. Pam: 'Now I know. You thought I was a little dorky.'
jokes.setup: Pam has been insisting she needs to know the real reason Danny didn't call back; Danny finally relents
jokes.punchline: 'Dorky' — delivered after a pause, as a simple, devastating single-word verdict. Pam's replay of it back to Danny confirms she received and processed it.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional in its economy. The whole episode builds to this revelation, and the payoff is a single syllable: 'Dorky.' The pause before it, Pam's calm repetition ('Now I know'), and the complete absence of drama from either party is the joke — the stakes were enormous, the answer is tiny and slightly insulting. The contrast between the buildup and the anticlimactic gentleness of 'dorky' is the peak of this storyline. One of the best-structured single-word punchlines in the series.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head after being called dorky: 'Well, excuse me.'
jokes.setup: Pam has just been told she seemed 'a little dorky' — the real reason Danny didn't call her back.
jokes.punchline: Her camera-to-talking-head response is just: 'Well, excuse me.' — delivered with just enough wounded dignity to be perfect.
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly capture Pam Beesly's character — defensive but restrained, slightly mortified, too dignified to be devastated. The talking-head format makes it land even harder because it's her confessing to the camera that she's bothered. Very high economy and character integration. Works as an emotional punctuation mark on the subplot.

jokes.text: Gabe's chain-of-command meeting devolves into an argument about a hat. Michael: 'We will put it in a hat and have Erin pick it out of the hat.' Darryl: 'I don't understand the point of the hat.' Michael: 'You're right. We don't need a hat.' Dwight: 'I am not budging on the hat issue.'
jokes.setup: They're trying to establish a decision-making protocol for future ideas.
jokes.punchline: Michael introduces a hat as a random decision mechanism, Darryl immediately rejects it, Michael folds, but then Dwight — who wasn't even the hat's inventor — refuses to budge on the hat.
jokes.explanation: The hat debate is a brilliant piece of absurdist escalation. The funniest beat is Dwight digging in on 'the hat issue' after Michael already abandoned it — Dwight defending a position the proposer has dropped is very Dwight. 'I am not budging on the hat issue' is a great line.

jokes.text: Gabe/Michael/Darryl chain of command negotiation ends with the hat proposal: 'We will put it in a hat and then we will have Erin pick it out of the hat and let her decide.' Darryl: 'I don't understand the point of the hat.' Michael: 'You're right, we don't need a hat.' Gabe: 'I am not budging on the hat issue.'
jokes.setup: Three-way negotiation over chain of command; Michael proposes a hat-based resolution
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately abandons the hat idea when challenged; Gabe immediately becomes immovable on the hat as a non-negotiable position
jokes.explanation: The hat negotiation is a micro-masterpiece of workplace absurdism. Michael proposes a random idea, abandons it instantly, and Gabe becomes passionate about the abandoned hat. The reversal — the proposer drops it and the objector commits — is structurally elegant. 'I am not budging on the hat issue' as a stance in a workplace negotiation is an excellent line.

jokes.text: After Michael and Darryl's reconciliation: 'Friends fight. Friends fight.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Darryl have just made up after a workplace dispute.
jokes.punchline: Michael summarizes the entire conflict with 'Friends fight. Friends fight.' — a phrase so simple and self-affirming it loops into absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Michael's childlike reduction of workplace conflict to 'friends fight' repeated twice is endearing and slightly unhinged. The repetition is the key — saying it once is a platitude, saying it twice makes it a mantra.

jokes.text: Andy's Cornell a cappella origin story: 'When I was a freshman in college, I worked at the student newspaper, the Cornell Daily Sun. This was at Cornell...'
jokes.setup: Darryl laments that he sometimes misses the warehouse. Andy tries to commiserate with a story about leaving something behind.
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'Cornell' story immediately includes the redundant clarification 'This was at Cornell' — the Cornell name-dropping is so reflexive he can't even stop himself in a self-help conversation.
jokes.explanation: Andy mentioning Cornell and then immediately clarifying 'This was at Cornell' in the same breath is a perfect piece of character comedy. His Cornell obsession is so deeply embedded that even when it's clearly Cornell he still feels compelled to specify. High character integration.

jokes.text: Andy: 'And that's actually when I heard eight male voices singing, unencumbered by instruments.' / Darryl: 'So is becoming CEO of this company your a cappella group?'
jokes.setup: Andy's Cornell story builds to the moment he found a cappella and abandoned journalism ambitions.
jokes.punchline: Darryl cuts to the analogy: 'So is becoming CEO of this company your a cappella group?' — completing Andy's tortured metaphor for him.
jokes.explanation: Darryl's dry reduction of Andy's winding Cornell story to a single devastating question is excellent. 'Is becoming CEO of this company your a cappella group?' is both a great line and a perfect Darryl moment — pragmatic, slightly contemptuous, efficient. The absurdity of equating corporate ambition with a cappella groups is also very funny. High economy and structure.

jokes.text: Jim's final talking head about Danny: 'To be honest, I still can't believe he didn't call her back. Who doesn't call a dork like that back?'
jokes.setup: The 'dorky' subplot has been resolved. Jim reflects on it.
jokes.punchline: 'Who doesn't call a dork like that back?' — Jim calling Pam a dork with pure affection, completely reclaiming the word.
jokes.explanation: The episode's most emotionally resonant joke. Jim calling Pam 'a dork like that' with complete adoration is the perfect button on the Danny subplot — it recontextualizes 'dorky' from an insult into a term of endearment. The structure is exceptional: the callback uses the episode's central insult to deliver the warmest possible punchline. This is The Office at its best — comedy that doubles as romantic character writing. Among the episode's top two or three moments.

jokes.text: Jim in his Popeye costume: 'Spinach in a can. Powerful spinach. A-gah-gah-gah-gah.' Pam: 'Aw, my hero.'
jokes.setup: Jim has finally put on the Popeye costume after resisting all episode.
jokes.punchline: He does the full Popeye spinach bit — 'A-gah-gah-gah-gah' — for Pam alone, after his romantic talking head.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Popeye costume subplot. Jim finally putting on the costume and doing the bit for Pam — after the 'dork' talking head — is structurally satisfying and genuinely charming. Pam's 'Aw, my hero' completes the emotional arc. Works as physical comedy and character comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: Oscar wins the costume contest. Oscar wins with his 'Rational Consumer' costume, beating out all the actual Halloween costumes.
jokes.setup: The costume contest results are announced. Everyone has worn real costumes — Dracula, nurse, Popeye, Lady Gaga, etc.
jokes.punchline: Oscar wins with 'Rational Consumer' — a sign and a concept, beating actual costumes with meta-commentary.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully complete episode-long joke. Oscar debunked the prize, made a costume out of his own skepticism, walked the catwalk with it, and won the very prize he'd spent the episode undermining. The irony is rich and the structural payoff across the episode is excellent. The fact that he wins the coupon book he logically dismantled is the perfect comedic circle.

jokes.text: Oscar's talking head explaining his vote: 'If I have to vote for someone I don't want it to be someone who can be me. Shake things up. I'm an inner guy.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has won. He explains his own voting strategy.
jokes.punchline: Oscar reveals he voted for himself as an act of anti-conformism — 'I'm an inner guy' — which is ironic given his highly analytical, rule-following nature.
jokes.explanation: Oscar's self-congratulatory explanation of his vote — framing voting for himself as edgy counter-programming — is mild irony. 'I'm an inner guy' as self-description is funny in its opacity.

jokes.text: Final talking head: 'Best Edward James [Olmos] costume I've ever seen. Like freaky good.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has won the costume contest with his 'Rational Consumer' costume.
jokes.punchline: Someone's talking head reveals they thought Oscar was dressed as Edward James Olmos — not 'Rational Consumer' — and are deeply impressed.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful button on the episode. Someone voted for Oscar's costume thinking he was dressed as Edward James Olmos (who resembles Oscar Martinez) — which means Oscar may have won on looks alone, not his clever concept. 'Like freaky good' is a great underline. This punctures Oscar's self-satisfaction perfectly and is a strong closing joke.

tmdb_overview: When Darryl takes an idea to corporate over his head, Michael freaks out. Everyone in the office is in a competitive mood as the Halloween costume contest gets underway. Meanwhile, Pam tries to get the truth out of Danny about their dating history.
